chapters.title: To the Republic of Geneva.
paragraphs: Magnificent, most honoured and sovereign Lords: Only a virtuous person, I am convinced, can honour his country in a way she can accept without shame. Accordingly, I have spent the last thirty years trying to become worthy of offering you a public tribute. The fortunate occasion now before me makes up, to a degree, for the shortcomings of my efforts. In approaching you, I have therefore felt entitled to follow the ardour that inspires me rather than measure the claim that should warrant my doing so. My life began among you, a piece of good fortune I cannot forget. How could I consider the equality that human beings owe to nature, or the inequality they have themselves created, without remembering the deep wisdom displayed by your state? It has happily reconciled the two, maintaining public order and safeguarding private happiness through arrangements that depart minimally from natural law while fulfilling the purposes of society as effectively as possible. When I asked myself which sound principles would best shape a perfect government, I was amazed to discover them all realised in yours. Even had my birthplace been beyond your walls, I would have considered it an unavoidable duty to dedicate this picture of human society to your people. In my opinion, no others enjoy so many of society's benefits or have protected themselves so successfully against its least abuses.

If choosing my birthplace had been within my power, I would have selected a community whose size matched the limits of human abilities: one, in other words, that could be governed well. Each member would be capable of performing his own duties, with no need to transfer to someone else the responsibility entrusted to him. I would have wanted a state whose subjects knew one another well enough for neither vice's secret plots nor virtue's unassuming modesty to escape public notice and judgment. Through the pleasant habit of meeting and knowing one another, each citizen's attachment to his country would be an affection for the people who lived there, more than for the ground they occupied.

I would have wished for birth in a country where the sovereign and the subjects shared a single interest, so that every movement of the machinery necessarily served the good of the whole. That can happen only where subjects and sovereign form the same person. My wish would therefore necessarily have been for a democratic government, moderated by wise restraints.

My choice would have been to live in freedom and to die in freedom. By that I mean being subject to laws whose honourable yoke neither I nor anyone else in the community could throw off. Such a yoke is beneficial and agreeable; the proudest necks bear it all the more willingly because they were never made to bear another.

Accordingly, I would have wanted no member of the state to boast that he stood higher than its laws, and no grounds for the state to fear having laws imposed on it by another power. Whatever form a government takes, a single man exempt from its laws necessarily leaves everyone else at his mercy (1). And when there are two heads, one native and one foreign, even the best possible division of sovereign power between them cannot enable both to be properly obeyed or the government to be properly conducted.

However excellent its laws, a recently established republic would not have attracted me. Its government might have been designed for circumstances quite different from the pressing needs and demands which it actually faced at that moment. I could have no assurance against its being convulsed and destroyed in its earliest days, whether through an administration unsuited to its subjects or subjects unsuited to the new administration. Freedom is like rich, substantial nourishment or a fine, potent wine: it sustains and fortifies healthy people whose bodies are used to it, but burdens, deranges and destroys weak, sensitive bodies unfamiliar with it. People who have once grown accustomed to living under masters afterwards discover that they cannot do without them. Their very efforts to loosen their bonds carry them further off the road to liberty. They confuse liberty with unrestricted licence, although the two are opposites. Almost invariably they finish enslaved to charlatans who, far from relieving their fetters, tighten them beyond anything previously endured. Consider even Rome, which later provided the pattern for all free states. On first escaping the Tarquins' dominion, the Romans lacked the capacity to rule themselves. Servitude and the humiliating work imposed by those tyrants had degraded them into an unthinking crowd. They initially needed indulgence and exceptionally wise direction. Gradual familiarity with freedom's health-giving air could alone restore souls enfeebled, indeed brutalised, by oppression's lash. In time they learned the austerity of behaviour and the nobility of courage which made them the earth's most respected nation. Thus I would have sought a contented and tranquil republic with origins already half-obscured by time's long darkness. Whatever disturbances it had undergone would have tested and strengthened its people's patriotism and bravery. After long experience of prudent independence, its citizens would be worthy of the freedom they possessed.

For my country I would have chosen a place protected from the savage fury of conquest by being fortunately unable to conquer, and still more fortunately situated so that it need not fear being conquered itself. It would be a free city among nations that saw no advantage in attacking its liberties, but instead considered themselves bound, for their own sake, to defend those liberties against others. In a word, it would be a republic offering nothing to excite its neighbours' ambitions, while having reasonable grounds to expect their help in an emergency. A republic placed so fortunately could fear only dangers arising within itself. If its members studied warfare, they would do so less from the need for defence than to keep alive the fighting ardour and generous spirit that so well accompany freedom and sustain an appropriate appreciation of it.

I would have looked for a country in which all inhabitants shared the power to make laws. Who could know better than the members of a community the terms on which they ought to live together? Yet I would not favour plebiscites of the Roman kind. Those excluded the commonwealth's leaders, the people most concerned with its preservation and prosperity, from deliberations on which its safety often rested. With an utterly absurd inconsistency, they denied magistrates privileges enjoyed by the humblest citizen.

My wish, on the contrary, would have been that individual citizens could not propose whatever laws happened to enter their heads. Reserving that privilege to magistrates would check self-serving, poorly considered schemes and dangerous innovations of the kind that finally ruined the Athenians. But the magistrates themselves would exercise it with great caution; the people would approve their proposals with great reserve; and the laws would then be proclaimed with such solemnity that, before they could endanger the constitution in any way, everyone would have time to grasp certain truths. Nothing does more to make laws sacred and respected than their great age. Ordinary people soon despise rules they see changed daily. And governments that learn to disregard ancient customs in the name of supposed improvements often introduce worse evils than those they meant to remedy or prevent.

Above all, I would have shunned a republic where the people claimed they could dispense with magistrates, or at least allow them only uncertain authority, and rashly kept the conduct of civil affairs and enforcement of their own laws in their own hands. Such a republic could hardly be well governed. That must have been the crude arrangement of the earliest governments as they emerged from the condition of nature; it was also another failing that helped bring the Athenian republic down.

My chosen community would instead be one whose private members asked only to ratify laws and decide the weightiest public business together, after hearing their magistrates' accounts. They would set up tribunals deserving of respect, carefully separate their jurisdictions, and choose, in yearly elections, the best-informed, most judicious and most honest men among them for the tasks of justice and government. The honesty of those officers would thus bear witness to the judgment of the people who selected them; each group would confer honour upon the other. Should serious misunderstandings ever interrupt the community's harmony and peace, even those intervals of error and blindness would show unmistakable evidence of mutual forbearance, mutual regard and universal reverence for the laws. Such signs would both promise and guarantee a heartfelt reconciliation that would last forever.

Magnificent, most honoured and sovereign Lords, these are the benefits I would have looked for if the choice of a native country had been mine. Suppose Providence had added a beautiful setting, a gentle climate, a productive soil and a prospect lovelier than any other beneath heaven. Then just one wish would remain before my happiness was complete: to possess these blessings while dwelling in that fortunate land. There I would share peaceful, pleasant companionship with my fellow citizens. Following their example as I dealt with them, I would fulfil the obligations of humanity, friendship and every other virtue, hoping that after my death I would be remembered as an honest man and a deserving patriot.

Less favoured by Providence, or taught wisdom by reflection only when it was too late, I might have been condemned to eke out my days, frail and listless, in a foreign climate. My sighs for quiet and repose would have been useless: I had thoughtlessly given them up when young. Nevertheless, I would have treasured inwardly the sentiments I have now declared, even without the chance to act upon them at home. A deep, disinterested tenderness for my faraway compatriots would have moved me to address them with complete sincerity, in words much like these.

Dear compatriots, let me rather call you dear brothers, for our kinship joins us quite as closely as our allegiance to a shared law. It delights me beyond measure that thoughts of you always bring thoughts of your blessings with them. Those blessings are lost to me, and perhaps that loss makes me value them more deeply than anyone who still possesses them. Each reflection upon your civic and political circumstances makes it harder for me to believe that anything better lies within the possibilities of nature. Elsewhere governments must gamble on imagined plans, or merely on things that might happen, even when their survival is at stake. For you, happiness has already been prepared. You need only take pleasure in it; satisfaction with being happy is all that complete happiness asks of you. By armed force you acquired, or recovered, your sovereignty. Wisdom and valour sustained it over two hundred years, and now every quarter fully recognises it. Most honourable treaties have defined the frontiers, secured the rights and guaranteed the rest you enjoy. Profound wisdom shaped your admirable and fortunate constitution, and powers of the highest standing guarantee it. Your public life is supremely tranquil: neither warfare nor conquest threatens you. You obey only your own wisely framed legislation, administered by honest officials of your own election. Your wealth does not reach the level at which luxury enervates people and frivolous pleasures destroy their relish for true contentment and firm virtue. Neither does poverty oblige you to ask outsiders to add to the produce of your labour. Finally, you keep your priceless liberty at scarcely any expense, while mighty nations can maintain theirs only at the cost of exorbitant taxation.

May this wisely ordered, fortunate republic long prosper, a blessing to its people and a pattern for humanity! There remains no other wish for you to form, no other concern on which to dwell. What lies ahead is entirely your responsibility: your forebears have already created your happiness, sparing you that labour, but you must preserve it by employing it well. Lasting concord, obedience to the laws and regard for their officers are the conditions of your survival. Hurry to eradicate the tiniest remaining germ of bitterness or suspicion; that cursed ferment would eventually and inevitably bring disaster and destruction upon the republic. I implore every one of you to search his deepest feelings and hear conscience's private counsel. Could a single citizen name, across the entire world, officials more honest, prudent, informed and honourable than your own? Surely each offers an exemplary model of self-restraint, plain living, legal obedience and wholehearted reconciliation. For your own sake, give such judicious leaders the unqualified confidence which rational people owe to virtue. You selected them; their performance honours that selection. Any distinction paid to the men you have raised to office must necessarily honour you as well. Surely nobody can be so unobservant as to miss this: if legislation becomes powerless and its guardians lose their standing, everybody's security and liberty disappear. What further demand is there upon you beyond undertaking gladly, without mistrust, the actions already required by your welfare, obligations and good sense? An indifferent attitude towards defending the constitution would be both blameworthy and perilous. Never let it lead you, in a moment of need, to disregard the considered advice of your most capable and devoted compatriots. Continue to act with justice, self-command and determination tempered by profound courtesy. Let humanity see a nation at once bold and unassuming, equally vigilant in guarding its glory and its independence. My final counsel is especially urgent: guard against spiteful constructions and venomous speech. The purposes concealed beneath them are frequently worse than the deeds they condemn. A household instantly rouses itself at the warning of a dependable, alert dog whose bark announces thieves and nothing else. By contrast, we detest the pestering of yapping curs that continually rob everyone of quiet. Their never-ending false alarms make it impossible to attend when one of their warnings happens to be timely.

To you particularly, Magnificent and most honoured Lords, I offer this expression of reverence and duty. You are the deserving and esteemed magistrates of a people living in freedom. Surely, if any position can add distinction to its occupant, it is one to which merit in both talent and virtue leads. Yours is just such a position: you have earned it, and your compatriots have conferred it upon you. Their excellence lends great additional brightness to your own. Your electors are men competent to rule others, yet they entrust you with ruling them. In my eyes, therefore, the distance between you and ordinary magistrates equals that between a free nation, especially the nation it is your privilege to preside over, and the populations of other countries in wisdom and understanding.

Let me recall a particular example, one that deserves more lasting traces than it has left and that my heart can never lay aside. Remembering the good citizen who gave me life always fills me with the most welcome emotion. In childhood I often heard him speak about the reverence you deserved. Even now I picture him supporting himself by manual labour while feeding his intelligence on truths of the highest order. The implements of his craft lie beside books by Tacitus, Plutarch and Grotius. A cherished son sits near him, listening to the tender teaching of a father without equal, and profiting from it far too little, alas! The escapades of a heedless youth temporarily drove those excellent lessons from my mind. Happily I have since experienced their lasting value: no matter how strongly a pupil is drawn towards wrongdoing, instruction from a deeply affectionate master can scarcely fail, at some point, to make him better.

Such, Magnificent and most honoured Lords, are your country's citizens and even its ordinary natives. Such are those knowledgeable, sensible men whom other nations, under the names of tradesmen and common people, habitually regard with contempt and entirely false assumptions. I gladly acknowledge that my father was in no way exceptional among his fellow citizens: he was simply what they all are. Yet nowhere would people have failed to seek his conversation; men of the highest station and greatest wealth would have cultivated his acquaintance, to their considerable advantage. It is not my place, and thank Heaven it is unnecessary, to tell you what regard you owe such men. They equal you in education as well as in nature and birth; they stand below you by their own choice, through the preference your merits deserved and received, a preference for which you in turn owe gratitude. I am delighted to hear how, in every dealing with them, your courtesy and approachability soften the gravity appropriate to officers of the law. Your esteem and concern for their welfare repay so well the respect and obedience they give you. How just and wise a course, fitted to efface ever more completely the memory of those unhappy events that ought to remain buried in everlasting silence and forgetfulness! It is all the more judicious because this fair-minded, generous people takes pleasure in duty and naturally enjoys honouring you. Those most eager to uphold their own rights and privileges are also the most willing to respect yours.

We naturally expect the directors of a civil community to care deeply for its welfare and renown. A rarer stroke of fortune occurs when men who regard themselves as officers, or indeed lords, of a loftier, holier homeland feel affection for the earthly homeland that feeds them. What pleasure to claim that unusual exception for ourselves! What pleasure to include among our worthiest citizens those devoted keepers of the sacred beliefs established by law, those venerable spiritual shepherds whose gentle, animated eloquence can root Gospel teaching in men's hearts all the better because they first practise its lessons themselves! Everyone is aware of the success with which the great skill of preaching from the pulpit is developed at Geneva. But the familiar spectacle of theologians preaching one course and following another makes people overlook something remarkable here: our whole ministry displays Christian feeling, upright conduct, strictness towards themselves and forbearance towards their neighbours. Perhaps Geneva alone, among all the cities of the world, can claim so complete and edifying a union of its men of letters with its teachers of religion. I place my hopes of the commonwealth's perpetual peace chiefly in their acknowledged judgment and restraint, and in their devotion to its flourishing. Their abhorrence of certain terrible doctrines gives me pleasure mingled with wonder and respect. History more than once presents those barbarous holy men who professed to uphold God's supposed rights while actually pursuing their own advantage. Believing their own blood secure from harm, they became correspondingly reckless in spilling the blood of others.

Can I leave out that precious half of our republic which makes the other half happy, and whose gentleness and prudent conduct do so much to preserve the blessings of peace and good behaviour? Beloved and virtuous women of our city, your sex will always be destined to govern ours. Happy! As long as your chaste authority, kept within marriage, serves only your country's honour and happiness! This was how women ruled at Sparta, and how you deserve to rule at Geneva. What man would be brutal enough to resist honour and reason when they speak through a loving wife? Who would not scorn luxury's hollow attractions on seeing your simple, modest clothes, which seem most favourable to beauty because of the radiance you lend them? Through your gracious, innocent influence and the quiet persuasion of your conversation, you must sustain harmony among citizens and a proper love and respect for their country's laws. Bring estranged families together through happy marriages. Above all, let your gently persuasive lessons and the modest grace of your speech correct the false ideas our young people acquire abroad. Instead of learning the many useful things available for observation and practice there, they bring home a childish manner and ridiculous airs picked up among dissolute women, together with admiration for some supposed grandeur, I hardly know what. It is a miserable compensation for slavery, utterly beneath comparison with the true, inherent greatness of majestic freedom. Remain what you are: the chaste protectors of our conduct and the gentle ties that keep our peace. On every occasion, continue to use the privileges of nature and affection to serve duty and virtue.

May nothing that happens ever prove me wrong in promising, on the strength of your mighty assistance, unending honour for the republic and contentment for its citizens. Still, I acknowledge that all our advantages cannot give our state the glittering appearance that dazzles most spectators. A childish and pitiable appetite for that glitter is prosperity's and freedom's most ruinous foe. Let wayward youths go abroad to find readily available delights followed by lingering remorse. Let would-be arbiters of taste marvel elsewhere at stately residences, elegant vehicles, lavish interiors, magnificent shows and every sophisticated indulgence of luxury and effeminacy. Geneva offers only human beings to look at; yet they are a sight with its own worth. Those who search for worth of this sort need not yield in value to the admirers of any other.

Magnificent, most honoured and sovereign Lords, I entreat you all to welcome these respectful signs of my fellow feeling for your common good with the same generosity. Perhaps, in allowing my heart to speak so freely, I have unfortunately strayed into an indiscreet excess of feeling. If so, I humbly ask forgiveness on behalf of a patriot's tender affection and the ardent, legitimate zeal of a man whose highest wish for his own happiness is that he may witness the happiness of you all.
With the deepest respect, Magnificent, most honoured and sovereign Lords, I remain your most humble and obedient servant and your fellow citizen, John James Rousseau. Chamberi, 12 June, 1754.
